t.1.170.2: Surely, dear sirs, your eyes have been taken away by that great-souled one in his anger as he remembered his slain kinsmen; of this there is no doubt.
t.1.170.1: I am not taking away your sight, my dear sons, nor am I filled with anger. But this Bhārgava, born from the thigh, is surely angry with you today.
t.1.170.4: For the entire Veda, together with its six auxiliary limbs, entered into him while he was still lying in the womb, out of a wish to do a further kindness to the lineage of Bhṛgu.
t.1.170.3: When you, my little sons, set about killing even the unborn children of the Bhṛgus, then I carried this child in my thigh for a hundred years.
t.1.170.5: Surely it is he who, out of anger over the slaying of his fathers, wishes to kill you, he by whose divine splendor your eyes have been taken away.
t.1.170.7: Thus addressed, all those kings then said to the thigh-born one, "Be gracious!" And he then showed them his grace.
t.1.170.6: Beg him, my dear, this Aurva, my most excellent son; satisfied by your prostration, he will release your sight.
t.1.170.8: That brahmin seer, best of the virtuous, was born by splitting open the thigh, and by this very name, Aurva, he became renowned throughout the worlds.
t.1.170.9: Then, having regained their eyesight, the kings went back from there; but the Bhārgava sage resolved upon the destruction of all the worlds.
t.1.170.12: With great and fierce austerity he scorched the worlds, together with gods, asuras and humans, intending to gladden his forefathers.
t.1.170.10: He, the great-minded one, my son, set his own mind wholly upon the destruction of all the worlds.
t.1.170.11: Wishing to exact vengeance for the Bhṛgus, that best of the Bhṛgus grew mighty through great austerity, bent on the destruction of all the worlds.
t.1.170.13: Then, my dear, the ancestors, having come to know of that best of the Bhṛgus, came from the world of the ancestors and all spoke these words.
t.1.170.14: Aurva, dear son, the might of you who are fierce through austerity has been seen; show favor to the worlds and restrain your own anger.
t.1.170.15: For it was not out of powerlessness, dear son, that the slaughter by the violent Kṣatriyas was then disregarded by all the Bhṛgus, whose selves were perfected.
t.1.170.16: For when weariness came upon us because of our exceedingly long life, then, dear son, we ourselves desired death at the hands of the kṣatriyas.
t.1.170.17: For that wealth was indeed buried in the house of the Bhṛgus by someone, placed there at that time solely to stir up enmity, by those who wished to provoke the kṣatriyas. For what need have we of wealth, we who seek heaven, O bull among the twice-born?
t.1.170.19: And a man who kills himself, dear son, does not attain the auspicious worlds; therefore, having considered it thus, we did not destroy ourselves by our own hand.
t.1.170.18: But when Death was in no way able to carry us off, then, dear son, this approved means was devised by us.
t.1.170.20: And what you wish to do, dear son, is not pleasing to us. Restrain this mind of yours from the evil destruction of all the worlds.
t.1.170.21: For no kṣatriyas whatsoever, nor the seven worlds, dear son, can defile the fiery splendor of our austerities; slay this anger that has risen up in you.
